summary: All three findings F-001, F-003, F-004 are substantively closed. Tests are non-tautological, assertions are meaningful, and no flakiness or mock drift observed. Minor observation on F-001 edit_text assertion (see N-001) — no action required.

notes: N-001 (observation, no action): The test monkeypatches `publish.Message` to `FakeCallbackMessage` so that `isinstance(callback.message, Message)` in publish.py:385 fires on the fake. This is correct and necessary — the production guard `isinstance(callback.message, Message)` is tested by the monkeypatch being present. However, if someone removes the monkeypatch line accidentally (e.g. during refactor), the test would still pass but the edit_text call might not happen (depending on whether the else-branch silently swallows). This is inherent to the monkeypatching approach and not a flaw in the current test. Observation only.
callback.answer('Rejected', None) assertion is present and correct — mirrors the approve test structure.

isolation_and_quality.flakiness: None observed. All tests use monkeypatching or FakeQueue with deterministic state. No time-dependent or network-dependent paths.

verdict_rationale: All three medium-severity findings are substantively closed. Tests assert real behavior: F-001 catches wrong CAS target, wrong edit text, and spurious publish/regenerate calls; F-003 catches a flipped conditional in _preview_keyboard via order-pinned exact list comparison; F-004 catches a README rewrite dropping the rotation runbook. No tautological tests, no reflexive asserts, no mock drift. Verdict: approve.
